newsitem.title: UK: EMU sweet and sour for Europe's banks - bankers.
newsitem.headline: EMU sweet and sour for Europe's banks - bankers.

text.p: A single currency will lead to a major consolidation and revenue erosion in European banking, top bankers said on Tuesday.
Structural changes are expected not just in investment banking, but also in the retail sector where increased competition will force banks to explore new avenues to attract business.

"We have overbanking in Europe. This is going to be subject to a great deal of pressure," said Dame Pauline Neville-Jones, managing director and global head of business strategy at Britain's NatWest Markets.
"Over time, we're going to have to get cleverer," she told Global 24, a conference on EMU linking participants around the world by video.

Bankers on a panel in London said Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would wipe out small, regional banks, while industry leaders would benefit from increased mobility of capital and technological revolution.
Operational efficiency would be crucial.
Neville-Jones said if the euro was dynamic and survived in a low interest rate environment, it would stimulate innovation in financial services and the technology of risk management.
Banks would have more incentive to dabble in exotic markets, and increase emphasis on mergers and acquisitions as well as advisory banking through the corporate restructuring process.
Competition would become tougher in personal asset and pension management, which would constitute a major chunk of investment banks' activity, bankers said.
Ronaldo H. Schmitz, board member at Deutsche Bank AG in Frankfurt, said retail banking would also be under pressure for change after currency borders are dismantled.
"Convergence of habits and tastes is a powerful force," he said, adding that banks would benefit from better exploiting opportunities across the European platform.
New products, such as European life insurance, could be introduced, he said.
"A high degree of open efficiency is needed in order to ease the squeeze in earnings," Schmitz said.
Neville-Jones said faced with lower returns on equity and capital, banks would have to put a premium on their management expertise and operational efficiency.
Tim Barker, vice-chairman at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London said EMU would, over a period of time, lead to a concentration of wholesale banks.
"But...this will be driven by what the customer wants and what cost will be saved as part of that process," he said.
If Britain stayed out of the single currency for a considerable time, London's position as the European centre for investment banking would be under threat, he added.
But despite the expected consolidation and short-term costs, the banking sector is likely to benefit from increased mobility and labour market restructuring, bankers said.
"The opportunities in Europe are huge and will be enhanced by EMU," said David Walker, executive chairman of Morgan Stanley in Europe.
